title: How the Concorde Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss the Concorde supersonic airliner: its origins as a British-French project amid 1960s supersonic transport (SST) races with the Soviets (Tupolev Tu-144, the "Concordski") and the Americans (Boeing 2707). They cover the Tu-144 crash at a Paris air show, the 2000 Air France Flight 4590 crash after a metal strip caused a tire blowout and fuel tank rupture, the plane's design (delta wing, droop nose, no horizontal stabilizer, engines mounted on the wing, fuel trimming for center-of-gravity shifts, heat-reflective paint), its cruising speed around Mach 2 at 60,000+ feet, afterburners, passenger experience and cost, Phil Collins's Live Aid flight, the program's financial losses, its retirement in 2003, and museums where Concordes can be seen. Also covers a listener mail from Stefan in Germany and a brief hurricane-coverage opening.

segments.title: Opening banter and Concorde museum visits
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about spelling Concorde, a hurricane-related weather coverage remark, and a Concorde at the Smithsonian Udvar-Hazy Center near Dulles, plus Josh's attempt to reach a former Concorde passenger.

segments.title: Origins of the supersonic transport race
segments.summary: In the early 1960s the British and French governments jointly pursued a supersonic transport, while the Soviets and Americans also pursued their own SSTs. The Soviet Tu-144 was nicknamed the Concordski. The American Boeing project was scrapped after cost and sonic boom concerns.

segments.title: Tu-144 crash at Paris air show
segments.summary: The hosts describe the Soviet Tu-144 crash at a Paris air show, in which the plane came apart while the pilot flew it aggressively, killing those on board and people on the ground.

segments.title: Air France Flight 4590 crash
segments.summary: The hosts recount the July 2000 Air France Concorde crash, caused by a metal strip left by a Continental jet that led to a blown tire, debris rupturing a fuel tank and fire, and a crash into a hotel. A Continental mechanic and a mechanic were convicted of manslaughter, later overturned in 2010.

segments.title: Concorde performance and aerodynamic design
segments.summary: Concorde cruised at about Mach 2 at 60,000 to 70,000 feet, roughly twice the altitude of a Boeing 747. Its design included a slender fuselage, delta wings with no horizontal stabilizer, and engines mounted directly to the wing. Comparisons to Chuck Yeager and Felix Baumgartner's high altitude jump are made.

segments.title: Droop nose, wings and passenger cabin
segments.summary: The droop nose lowered for takeoff and landing for pilot visibility and raised for supersonic flight. The visor protected the windscreen. The cabin was narrow with two-by-two seating and identical cabin classes, and the hosts discuss blankets and washing.

segments.title: Engines, afterburners and fuel consumption
segments.summary: Concorde used four Rolls-Royce/Snecma Olympus engines with afterburners (reheat) to reach supersonic speed. Fuel consumption was very high, burning kerosene at about a ton per passenger. The Soviet Tu-144 needed afterburners on throughout flight.

segments.title: Fuel trim system and heat-reflective paint
segments.summary: Concorde moved fuel between trim tanks to keep its center of gravity balanced as it shifted at supersonic speed. Its special white paint reflected heat because the nose could reach very high temperatures from air friction.

segments.title: Passenger experience, cost and Phil Collins's Live Aid flight
segments.summary: A round trip cost around 12,000 dollars in 1980s money. Passengers got lounges, service and signed certificates. Phil Collins flew the Concorde from London to New York to play Live Aid in Philadelphia after the Wembley show, using the time difference to arrive before he left. Fred Finn took 718 flights.

segments.title: Concorde economics and retirement
segments.summary: Concorde lost money from the start, and British and French governments continued the project partly to avoid lawsuits. Operations ended in 2003 after the 2000 crash and financial pressures. Comparisons are drawn to Reagan-era suborbital transport ideas and SpaceX plans.

segments.title: Museums where Concorde can be seen
segments.summary: The hosts list places to see a Concorde, including the Smithsonian Udvar-Hazy Center, Aerospace Bristol, Le Bourget, the Intrepid museum in New York, Speyer in Germany, and the Museum of Flight in Seattle.

segments.title: Listener mail from Stefan in Germany
segments.summary: Stefan from Stuttgart, Germany writes that he is improving his English by listening to the show, which he found through old episodes on a Spotify playlist. The hosts respond.
